newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: LUKoil in hunt for oil in Azeris' Caspian sector. [CORRECTED 16:03 GMT]
newsitem.headline: LUKoil in hunt for oil in Azeris' Caspian sector. [CORRECTED 16:03 GMT]

text.p: Russia's biggest oil company LUKoil strengthened its position in the Caspian region on Wednesday, signing a memorandum with Azerbaijan's state oil firm and talking with other firms on developing oil in the region.

Vagit Alekperov, LUKoil president, told reporters the firm had signed a memorandum with the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) on Wednesday to begin talks on joint exploration and development of the Yalama offshore oil field in the Caspian.
LUKoil was also interested in working with SOCAR, Chevron of the United States and Rosneft of Russia on other projects in the Azeri sector of the Caspian, he said.

Alekperov pegged recoverable oil reserves at the Yalama field at up to 50 million tonnes. (corrects from Yamala) The field is about 25 km (15miles) wide and 30 km (20 miles) long, and straddles the Azeriand Russian sectors of the Caspian.

"It is difficult to say (about reserves) because there are no geophysical details or wells there, but according to our estimates we think there could be up to 50 million in obtainable reserves," he said.
LUKoil also has a stake in three other joint projects with SOCAR to develop offshore Caspian fields.
Similar memoranda in the past between SOCAR and foreign oil companies have led to the signing of fully-fledged drilling and production-sharing contacts.
Alekperov said that under the memorandum, a 90-day negotiating period to draw up a formal production sharing agreement between SOCAR and LUKoil would commence.
He gave no estimate of the possible investment in exploring or developing the field.

He said negotiations were continuing with SOCAR on joint development of the Inam offshore Caspian oil field, about 120 km southeast of the capital Baku, with reserves estimated by the Azeris at about 200 million tonnes.
LUKoil was also in talks with Chevron on forming a consortium with SOCAR to develop the Zeinalabdin Tagiyev field, which lies about 120 km (75 miles) south of Baku.
SOCAR estimates probable reserves in the field at 115 million tonnes of oil and 425 million cubic meters of gas.
"We haven't finished negotiations with them yet, but we would very much like to work with Chevron," said Alekperov.
LUKoil was discussing joint Caspian development projects in the Azeri sector of the Caspian with Russia's state-owned oil company Rosneft.
Rosneft has had no previous production involvement in Azerbaijan offshore oil projects, citing differences between Moscow and Baku over the Caspian Sea's status.
But Rosneft Pesident Alexander Putilov held talks with Azeri President Haydar Aliyev earlier this month, after which Aliyev urged the company to boost its activity in the region.
Russia and Iran, which both border the Caspian, claim it is a large lake whose resources must be jointly developed.
Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan say it is a sea and should be divided up into sectors and exploited by each country as such.
The status of the Caspian is further complicated by recent Turkmen claims to oil fields already under development and claimed as part of the Azeri sector of the Caspian.

Foreign oil companies have rushed to Azerbaijan since it gained independence from Moscow in 1991, signing agreements with the Azeri government worth over $15 billion to develop offshore Caspian fields.
